introduction-the-hidden-cloud-tax.core: Cloud providers charge little or nothing for data in, but bill data out to the internet, across regions, across availability zones and through NAT gateways. Those charges are invisible in architecture diagrams but can exceed compute costs for data-heavy systems. Egress cost engineering means knowing which paths cost what, then designing traffic to take the cheapest acceptable one.

first_principles.problem: A logging pipeline's data transfer bill is three times its compute bill, and nobody knows why.
truths: Ingress is free, egress is not.

analogy.title: Free entry, paid exit car park
analogy.story: Getting in costs nothing, but every exit has a fee, and some exits cost more than others.
analogy.breaks: Car parks show fees at exits; cloud fees show up a month later.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Reveals NAT bytes and cross-AZ as top costs.

code.text:
SELECT line_item_usage_type, SUM(line_item_unblended_cost) AS cost
FROM cur
WHERE line_item_usage_type LIKE '%DataTransfer%' OR line_item_usage_type LIKE '%NatGateway-Bytes%'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY cost DESC LIMIT 10;

check.q: Why are egress costs often missed in design reviews?
check.a: Architecture diagrams show components, not byte volumes or the per-GB price of each path between them.

the-hierarchy-of-cost.core: Rough AWS price tiers for data transfer, from cheapest: same-AZ private IP (free); VPC gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB (free); cross-AZ ($0.01/GB each way, $0.02 round trip); interface endpoints and PrivateLink (~$0.01/GB plus hourly); NAT gateway processing ($0.045/GB on top of other charges); cross-region (~$0.02/GB); internet egress (~$0.05–0.09/GB). Design to push traffic up this hierarchy.

first_principles.problem: Engineers can't estimate whether a design change saves money because they don't know relative path prices.
derivation: Use **PrivateLink** instead of NAT for AWS APIs.

analogy.title: Postage rates
analogy.story: Hand delivery next door is free, local post is cheap, international express is expensive, and some routes add surcharges.
analogy.breaks: Postage is per item; cloud is per GB and stacks across hops.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Path choice changes cost by orders of magnitude.

check.q: Why can NAT gateway traffic to S3 be doubly wasteful?
check.a: You pay NAT processing per GB when a free S3 gateway endpoint could carry the same traffic.

the-nat-gateway-trap.core: Private subnets often route 0.0.0.0/0 through a NAT gateway, so everything outbound, including S3, ECR image pulls, CloudWatch logs and package downloads, is charged $0.045/GB in processing. Container platforms pulling large images and log shippers can push terabytes through NAT. A NAT in another AZ adds cross-AZ charges too. The fixes are endpoints, per-AZ NATs and caching.

first_principles.problem: An EKS cluster pulling images from ECR racks up $8,000/month in NAT gateway processing.
truths: Default routes send everything to NAT.
derivation: Add **S3 gateway endpoint** (ECR layers live in S3).
Add **interface endpoints** for ECR API, logs, STS.

analogy.title: Paying a toll for trips to the shop next door
analogy.story: All roads out of your street pass a toll booth, even trips to the neighbour's shop that has a free back gate.
analogy.breaks: Tolls are visible; NAT charges appear only on the bill.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Image pulls and logs bypass NAT entirely.

points: AWS traffic through NAT is waste.

check.q: Why does an ECR image pull need an S3 gateway endpoint to fully avoid NAT?
check.a: ECR stores image layers in S3, so layer downloads go to S3 even when ECR API endpoints exist.

solution-1-gateway-endpoints-the-free-lu.core: Gateway VPC endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB. They're route-table entries that send traffic for those services' prefix lists directly over AWS's network, with no hourly or per-GB charge. Add them to every private route table, and use endpoint policies and bucket policies (aws:SourceVpce) to restrict access, which improves both cost and security.

first_principles.problem: A data lake reads 200 TB/month from S3 through NAT gateways, costing $9,000 in processing fees.
truths: They work by routing, not ENIs.

analogy.title: A free private tunnel to the warehouse
analogy.story: Instead of driving through the toll gate, a tunnel goes straight to the warehouse at no charge.
analogy.breaks: Tunnels are physical; gateway endpoints only work in-region.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Free path and bucket reachable only via the endpoint.

check.q: Can on-premises clients use an S3 gateway endpoint over Direct Connect?
check.a: No, gateway endpoints only serve traffic originating in the VPC; on-prem needs an S3 interface endpoint.

solution-2-interface-endpoints-privateli.core: Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) place ENIs with private IPs in your subnets for most AWS services and third-party or internal services. With private DNS, the service hostname resolves to those IPs. They cost about $0.01/hour per AZ plus ~$0.01/GB, much cheaper than NAT's $0.045/GB at volume, and keep traffic off the internet. With many services and VPCs, centralise them in a shared VPC.

first_principles.problem: Thousands of instances call SQS, KMS and Secrets Manager through NAT gateways, costing more than the services themselves.
truths: Per-GB cost is lower than NAT.
Hourly cost adds up across many endpoints and AZs.
derivation: **Centralise** endpoints in a hub VPC for many VPCs.

analogy.title: A private service counter inside your office building
analogy.story: Instead of travelling to the bank, a branch counter opens in your lobby for a small rent.
analogy.breaks: Counters serve one building; centralised endpoints need DNS sharing across VPCs.

example.title: Break-even
flow: SQS at 5 TB/mo: saves ~$170/mo per service

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: High-volume services pay for themselves quickly.

check.q: When might an interface endpoint cost more than using NAT?
check.a: For very low-volume services, where the hourly per-AZ charge exceeds the NAT per-GB savings.

zone-affinity-keeping-traffic-local.core: Cross-AZ traffic costs $0.01/GB in each direction and adds latency. Chatty microservices spread evenly across AZs send most calls across zones by default. Zone affinity routes requests to same-AZ backends when they're healthy and have capacity: Kubernetes topology-aware routing (trafficDistribution: PreferClose), Envoy/Istio locality load balancing, ALB cross-zone settings, and AZ-aware Kafka consumers (rack awareness).

first_principles.problem: A microservices mesh generates 400 TB/month of cross-AZ traffic, costing $8,000.
truths: Random balancing crosses AZs ~2/3 of the time (3 AZs).
Affinity must not overload a zone.

analogy.title: Shopping at the store in your own neighbourhood
analogy.story: Use the local branch when it's open and stocked; cross town only if it's closed.
analogy.breaks: Shops don't need balanced customers; skewed AZ capacity overloads pods.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Most calls stay in-zone; cross-AZ bill drops sharply.

code.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: orders }
spec:
  selector: { app: orders }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
  trafficDistribution: PreferClose   # same-zone endpoints when available

check.q: Why must zone-affine routing keep capacity balanced across AZs?
check.a: If one zone has fewer backends, keeping its traffic local can overload them while other zones sit idle.
